Golfinopoulos ⁎ M. Soupioni M. Kanellaki A.A. Koutinas University of Patras, Greece ⁎ Corresponding author. Keywords 14C-labeled lactose kefir lactose uptake delignified cellulosic materials The present work aims on determining pH effect on lactose uptake rate by kefir cells immobilized on delignified cellulosic materials during whey fermentation. Kefir yeast is a mixed culture consisting of various yeasts (Kluyeveromyces, Candida, Saccharomyces, Pichia) and lactic acid bacteria of the genus Lactobacillus. Yeast and lactic acid bacteria co-exist in a symbiotic association and are responsible for lactose fermentation of milk and whey. Whey is the liquid by-product of cheese production which contains proteins, fats and mainly carbohydrates (lactose∼5%). In order to examine the effect of pH on lactose uptake rate by kefir cells immobilized on delignified cellulosic materials, 14C-labeled lactose was used. This is a very convenient laboratory method as labeled and unlabeled molecules of the same species undergo exactly the same chemical reactions or follow the same metabolic pathways. The employed kefir culture was a commercial product which was grown in sterilized synthetic medium consisting of lactose 2%, yeast extract 0.4%, (NH4)2SO4 0.1%, KH2PO4 0.1% and MgSO4.7H2O 0.5% at 30oC and pH 5.5. Delignified cellulosic material was prepared from sawdust treated by 1% w/v NaOH for 3h at the boiling point, in order lignin to be removed. For the immobilization, 170g of delignified cellulosic material were added in an 800mL culture medium containing 12% lactose and 16g of wet weight kefir culture and allowed to ferment about 12h. Using 122g of wet immobilized biocatalyst a series of fermentations were carried out in 250mL of whey. At the beginning of each run a small quantity of 14C-labeled lactose was added. The experiments were conducted at various pH values (4, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5) at 30°C. The labeled lactose was fermented in the same way as the non-active one. Fermentation kinetics were monitored by determination of unfermented lactose with HPLC. The amount of the consumed labeled lactose was measured by liquid scintillation during certain time intervals of the fermentation and expressed as cpm lactose per gram of biomass per hour. The results illustrated that the lactose uptake rates are higher at pH 5.5.
